records.name: Confounding by indication
records.tldr: People often receive different treatments because their health or cancer differs. Those starting differences can distort a comparison of outcomes between treatments.
records.summary: A primary observational breast cancer study examined how treatment selection could make chemotherapy appear associated with recurrence and how adjustment methods changed the estimate. Measured-covariate adjustment did not eliminate the study's concern about residual confounding. A treatment association in routine-care data must be interpreted with the reasons treatment was selected. Propensity scores and large sample size do not automatically reproduce random assignment.

links.label: Treatment-selection confounding in an observational breast cancer study (2009)
Specifying a target trial prevents immortal time bias and other self-inflicted injuries in observational analyses
The Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) statement: guidelines for reporting observational studies.

notes: Confounding by indication arises when a reason for choosing treatment also relates to the outcome, such as giving more intensive therapy to people with more severe disease. Baseline fitness, access and prior care can also influence both treatment selection and outcome. A treatment-outcome association alone does not separate those pathways from the effect of treatment. The causal role and timing of each variable require the actual study context.

Fictional six-week symptom example: each treatment group contains 100 people. With A, 60 of 80 people in better baseline health improve and 5 of 20 in poorer health improve. With B, the corresponding counts are 15 of 20 and 20 of 80. Within each health category both treatments therefore have the same rates, 75 and 25 per cent, yet the pooled rates are 65 and 35 per cent because the baseline mixtures differ. This arithmetic illustrates a confounding explanation, not a recipe showing that matching one factor fixes every real comparison. Other differences, imperfect measurements, missing follow-up and clocks still matter.

records.name: Biomarker cutoff selection and validation
records.tldr: The threshold used to call a test positive is part of the test's evidence. A cutoff selected because it looked best in one dataset needs evaluation beyond that same dataset.
records.summary: The primary Cutoff Finder study demonstrated methods that optimize biomarker thresholds against distributions, outcomes or survival. Such an optimized split is a discovery result. Its performance must retain the selection procedure and be assessed with appropriate independent evaluation before a clinical rule is claimed. The assay scale and intended decision also matter: a threshold chosen for one drug or purpose is not automatically transferable to another.

links.label: FDA: reporting results of diagnostic-test studies
Dichotomizing continuous predictors in multiple regression: a bad idea
FDA: statistical guidance for reporting diagnostic-test studies

notes: A cutpoint applies a category rule to a continuous measurement. Analytical thresholds concern detection or quantitation; diagnostic thresholds classify a defined reference condition; protocol entry cutoffs determine eligibility; treatment-selection thresholds require evidence for an action. Detectable, quantifiable, positive and actionable are separate claims. Categorizing a continuous score does not make biology binary or imply a sharp switch across the line. Nor are cutoffs automatically interchangeable across assays, scales, model versions, drugs or intended uses.

Keep continuous measurements, reference outcomes, intended action, exact cutoff, units, direction, boundary equality, missing-result handling and assay or model version. Report counts and performance uncertainty. In a fixed fully assessed dataset where higher scores are positive, lowering the cutoff cannot lose an existing positive call, but may find extra cases and add false calls; performance can stay unchanged across an empty score range. Selecting the most favourable outcome-based cutoff can exaggerate separation and discard continuous information. Disclose the search, lock the rule and independently evaluate it in a relevant population for the intended action. Statistical separation alone does not establish clinical benefit.

Fictional scores for four reference-affected samples are 0.20, 0.55, 0.75 and 0.90; six unaffected samples have 0.10, 0.25, 0.35, 0.45, 0.60 and 0.80. Count equality as positive. At score at least 0.7: TP 2, FP 1, FN 2, TN 5, giving sensitivity 50 per cent, specificity 83.3 per cent and PPV 66.7 per cent. At least 0.4: TP 3, FP 3, FN 1, TN 3, giving sensitivity 75 per cent, specificity 50 per cent and PPV 50 per cent. Lowering this cutoff finds one additional affected sample and creates two additional false calls; sensitivity alone does not choose the better clinical action.

A mathematical optimization is only as appropriate as its stated objective and error costs. Using the same fictional counts, stipulate cost 5 for a missed case and 1 for a false call: the 0.7 rule costs 11 units and the 0.4 rule 8. Reverse the emphasis to costs 1 and 10, and the totals become 12 and 31. The preferred rule changes without changing any test result. These invented costs are not clinical valuations; actual decisions require relevant benefits, harms and evidence, not a universal mathematical maximum.
